cas.al.alumina_energy.locator: Alumina refining fuel table, 2019: heavy oil 842, diesel 7, natural gas 2,478, coal 6,414, electricity 547, other 168 MJ/t Al2O3
cas.al.alumina_energy.note: MJ per t alumina; summed as reported (electricity, 5 % of the total, is not converted to primary). Bounds are an assumption.

cas.al.alumina_per_al.note: t alumina per t primary aluminium; stoichiometric minimum 1.89 (Al2O3 / 2 Al = 101.96 / 53.96) plus small losses. The IAI LCI table that gives the value did not extract.

cas.al.smelting_electricity.note: PENDING IAI statistics (JS-gated): https://international-aluminium.org/statistics/primary-aluminium-smelting-energy-intensity/ (world AC intensity). Range '13-15 MWh of electricity' per tonne from trade press (AlCircle 2025).

cas.al.water.locator: Freshwater consumption 2019: alumina refining 5.4 m3/t Al ingot; smelting 5.6 m3/t Al ingot

cas.ammonia_per_explosive.note: t NH3 per t ANFO, from stoichiometry: ANFO is 94 % ammonium nitrate, and NH4NO3 needs 2 x 17.03 / 80.04 = 0.4255 t NH3 per t when its nitric acid is also made from ammonia; 0.94 x 0.4255 = 0.400. Emulsions have similar ammonium nitrate content (bounds: 85-100 % AN, assumption).

cas.ce.electricity.locator: p. 15 chart 'Electricity intensity of cement, 2014-50, kWh/t cement': 91 (2014), citing IEA Technology Roadmap (2018)
cas.ce.electricity.note: Low bound = the roadmap's 2050 value; high bound is an assumption for older plants.

cas.ce.kiln_thermal.locator: Milestones table: kiln thermal energy intensity 3.6 GJ per tonne of clinker (2022)
cas.ce.kiln_thermal.note: MJ per t clinker. Bounds are an assumption.

cas.ce.limestone_per_clinker.note: t raw meal (mostly quarried limestone) per t clinker; standard kiln mass balance (CaCO3 loses 44 % as CO2).

cas.cu.grinding_steel_per_ore.locator: Grinding balls 390 g/t ore (SAG) and 535 g/t (ball mills); liners 40 g/t (SAG) and 12 g/t (ball); Chile total 445 kt/yr (2014)
cas.cu.grinding_steel_per_ore.note: kg steel per t ore milled. High = SAG plus ball circuit (0.98 kg/t); low = ball-mill-only circuit (0.55 kg/t); central = midpoint.

cas.cu.loading_wear_per_rock.locator: '3.2 grams of steel for each tonne of material moved' (loading wear parts)

cas.cu.secondary_energy.note: PENDING. Primary energy per kg of copper refined from scrap (re-melting, fire refining, electrorefining). Open item since Phase 1; Wang et al. 2021 (ES&T 55:5485) give per-unit values only in their SI, and low-grade scrap needs more than double the energy of no. 2 scrap.

cas.cu.water_per_ore.locator: Concentration m3/t ore, 2009-2017 series 0.67 ... 0.45 (2017 value 0.45; 2009 value 0.69)
cas.cu.water_per_ore.note: Chilean concentrator unit water consumption. Hydrometallurgy is lower (0.11 m3/t in 2017); concentrators dominate. Seawater was 19 % of mining water in Chile in 2017.

cas.cu_energy_net_of_inputs.note: 1 = treat the Phase 1 copper energy (Norgate gross energy requirement, cradle-to-gate) as including the energy embodied in the modelled consumables (steel, explosives, water), and net it out of the copper column to avoid double counting in the cascade. 0 = treat it as direct energy only. Whether Norgate & Jahanshahi's inventory covers these consumables is not stated in the parts read.

cas.electricity_primary_factor.locator: Table 2.1.2 note, p. 7: primary energy includes generation, transmission and distribution losses of 67 % (1 / 0.33 = 3.03)
cas.electricity_primary_factor.note: MJ primary per MJ electricity. Same convention as the steel route energies. Low bound 2.5 (40 % efficient supply) is an assumption reflecting today's more efficient fleet.

cas.en.aluminium_share.locator: Fig. 2 (2007): electrical cable 3.8 Mt of 45 Mt aluminium in end-use goods
cas.en.aluminium_share.note: Share of aluminium used for power cables; a_al,en = share x aluminium output / primary energy, held at 2025 values. Bounds are an assumption.

cas.en.coal_explosives_per_t.locator: Table 3, 2018: coal mining 1,020 kt explosives; US coal production 755 million short tons = 685 Mt (EIA 2019)
cas.en.coal_explosives_per_t.note: kg explosives per t coal, US 2018. The US mines much of its coal at the surface, so this is likely an upper value for the world; the low bound (one third) is an assumption for a world mix with more underground mining.

cas.en.coal_per_mj.note: PENDING. t coal mined per MJ of world primary energy: about 9 Gt coal per year over 600 EJ. Global coal tonnage not yet sourced (IEA Coal 2025 or the Energy Institute Statistical Review would give it).

cas.en.copper_share.locator: p. 47, End-Use: Infrastructure 16 % (2019); same value as cu.share.infrastructure
cas.en.copper_share.note: Share of refined copper used by energy supply; a_cu,en = share x refined copper / primary energy, held at 2025 values. The ICA 'infrastructure' category is understood to cover power utility and telecommunication networks (category definition not stated in the factbook text; unverified). It includes telecom but excludes copper in generators and motors (industry), so these partly offset. Bounds are an assumption.

cas.en.own_use.locator: World energy balance 2019: TES 606.5 EJ; energy industry own use 37.0 EJ; losses 9.6 EJ ((37.0 + 9.6) / 606.5)
cas.en.own_use.note: MJ per MJ supplied. Power-plant conversion losses are excluded because they are already in the primary-energy factors. Low bound = own use only.

cas.en.steel_use.locator: 'World oil and gas pipe demand to reach 51.8 million metric tons in 2017' (low bound)
cas.en.steel_use.note: Steel used by energy supply per year (Mt/yr). Oil and gas pipe alone is the low bound; the central value adds an assumed ~30 Mt/yr for power plants, wind turbines, towers and transmission; high bound is an assumption.

cas.en.water_consumption.locator: p. 19: energy-sector water consumption 48 bcm in 2014, about 12 % of its 398 bcm withdrawals
cas.en.water_consumption.note: Consumption, not withdrawals: once-through cooling withdrawals are mostly self-supplied and returned. Divided by the 2025 primary energy for a_wa,en. Bounds +/- 30 % (assumption).

cas.nh.energy.locator: p. 26: 8.6 EJ energy consumption in 2020; p. 16: 185 Mt ammonia produced in 2020 (8.6 EJ / 185 Mt = 46.5 GJ/t, feedstock included); low = best available gas technology 28 GJ/t (p. 11)

cas.powder_factor.locator: Memo 27 June 2012: design powder factor 0.96 kg/m3 = 0.35 kg/t at 2.77 t/m3 (one open-pit copper-gold design)
cas.powder_factor.note: kg explosive per t of rock blasted, applied to copper ore and waste rock, iron ore and limestone. The bounds are an assumption spanning soft quarry rock to hard porphyry; only one project figure was sourced.

cas.st.ore_per_primary_iron.locator: Iron ore chapter: world usable ore 2,600 Mt (2025e); iron and steel chapter: world pig iron 1,300 Mt (2025e)
cas.st.ore_per_primary_iron.note: t usable ore per t primary iron. Low bound allows for direct reduced iron (not in MCS), which adds to primary iron from the same ore.

cas.st.rock_per_ore.note: t rock blasted (crude ore plus waste) per t usable iron ore. MCS gives crude ore only for the US (crude/usable about 2.5-3 there); no global strip ratio was found.

cas.st.water_bf_bof.locator: Integrated plants: intake 28.6 m3/t, discharge 25.3 m3/t (2011 member survey); consumption = difference

cas.st.water_eaf.locator: EAF plants: intake 28.1 m3/t, discharge 26.5 m3/t (2011 member survey); consumption = difference

cas.wa.desal_electricity.locator: Introduction: SWRO 'between 3.5 and 4.5 kWh m-3 to produce product water' (full range 3-6.7)

cas.wa.desal_share.locator: Global desalination 'over 95 million m3 day-1' in 2016 (GWI 2016): 34.7 bcm/yr of 4,000 bcm withdrawals
cas.wa.desal_share.note: Share of supplied water that is desalinated; the scenario lever for mining's move to seawater. IEA 2016 p. 31: re-use and desalination supply 'less than 1% of all water needs'. Bounds are an assumption.

cas.wa.energy_conventional.locator: p. 30: 120 Mtoe used in the water sector in 2014, about 60 % as electricity (~820 TWh), the rest thermal
cas.wa.energy_conventional.note: Primary MJ per m3 of conventionally supplied water. Average: (820 TWh x 3.6 PJ/TWh x 3.03 + (5,024 - 2,952) PJ thermal) / 4,000 bcm = 2.75 MJ/m3; desalination removed: (2.75 - 0.0087 x 43.6) / (1 - 0.0087) = 2.40, where 43.6 MJ/m3 = 4.0 kWh/m3 x 3.6 x 3.03. Counts supply, treatment, distribution and wastewater; excludes in-field irrigation and water heating (Box 2). Bounds are an assumption.

cas.wa.global_withdrawal.locator: p. 19: energy-sector withdrawals 398 bcm in 2014; pp. 5 and 12: energy accounts for 'around 10% of global water withdrawals'
cas.wa.global_withdrawal.note: Global water withdrawals (m3/yr); also the 2025 output of the water sector (held at the 2014 level; assumption).

cas.x2025.aluminium.locator: Aluminum chapter: world primary smelter production 74,000 kt (2025e)

cas.x2025.ammonia.locator: Nitrogen chapter: world ammonia 160,000 kt N (2025e); x 17.03 / 14.01 = 194.5 Mt NH3

cas.x2025.energy.locator: Global primary energy 'just over 600 EJ' in 2025

cas.x2025.steel.locator: Iron and steel chapter: world raw steel 1,900 Mt (2025e)

cc.biogenic_share.note: Share of the stream's carbon that is biogenic (matrix and reductant).

cc.capture_fraction.note: Share of the carbon-cup CO2 stream captured.

cc.carbon_per_metal.note: kg of carbon in the burnable matrix per kg of copper housed.

cc.collection.note: Share of end-of-life copper in cups that reaches combustion with ash recovery. Low = today's copper collection rate (cu.eol_collection_rate).

cc.matrix_net_energy.note: Energy to make the matrix, net of energy recovered by burning it, per kg of carbon. Negative = net energy recovered.

cc.processing.note: Share of collected cup copper recovered as metal from the ash.

cc.t_max.note: Highest temperature of the ash-reduction step (1500 C; range 1200-1600 C, the span of copper/lead smelting and steelmaking). Sets Ellingham eligibility.

cu.eol_collection_rate.note: Mean 0.67, SD 0.07 over 2002-2012; bounds are mean +/- 2 SD.

cu.eol_processing_rate.note: Mean 0.69, SD 0.01; bounds are mean +/- 2 SD. Collected EoL copper not processed into old scrap goes to 'other scrap markets' (largely steel and aluminium scrap streams).

cu.eol_recycling_rate_reported.locator: Tabelle 5.3, p. 114 (EoL RR = i/e; mean 2002-2012, SD 0.05)
cu.eol_recycling_rate_reported.note: Calibration target, not a model input. Should equal collection x processing to within rounding (0.67 x 0.69 = 0.462).

cu.fabrication_loss_fraction.note: True losses at fabrication and manufacturing / semis = (150 + 200) / 25,250 kt.

cu.fabrication_yield.locator: Supplementary Data, sheet '1. Data - Process yields (m)', row 29_Cu
cu.fabrication_yield.note: Final goods / semis: 20,850 / 25,250 in S11. The shortfall is mostly new scrap that returns (see cu.new_scrap_recovery).

cu.in_use_dissipation_fraction.note: In-use dissipation / final goods = 450 / 20,850 kt. Applied to inflow; Charpentier Poncelet assign it by sector (chemicals 100 %, transport 0.4 %, construction 0.2 %).

cu.lifetime_sigma_fraction.note: Gaussian lifetime distributions with SD = 15 % of the expected value.

cu.new_scrap_capture.note: Share of manufacturing residue (semis - final goods) recovered as new scrap = 4,200 / (25,250 - 20,850) kt; the rest (200 kt) is manufacturing loss. Product-group residue comes from cu.fab_efficiency.*.

cu.new_scrap_recovery.locator: Supplementary Data, sheet '1. Data - Process yields (m)', row 29_Cu
cu.new_scrap_recovery.note: Share of fabrication residues recovered as new scrap.

cu.production_yield.locator: Supplementary Data, sheet '1. Data - Process yields (m)', row 29_Cu
cu.production_yield.note: Taken by Charpentier Poncelet from Helbig 2020 / Glöser-Chahoud 2017. Equals refined copper / (Cu in ore + low-quality scrap) in S11: 19,700 / (19,800 + 3,800).

cu.scrap_to_smelter_share.note: Share of the scrap pool (old + new) that is low quality and goes back through smelting/refining = 3,800 / 9,400 kt; the remainder (5,600 kt) is high-quality scrap melted directly by semis makers.

cu.semis_loss_fraction.note: Fabrication losses at semis production / semis = 150 / 25,250 kt.

cu.share.construction.locator: p. 47, 'Major Uses of Copper, 2019', End-Use: Building Construction

cu.share.consumer.note: -> Konsum & Elektronik (4 groups). ICA 'Equipment' is the closest match; the mapping is approximate.

cu.tailings_share_of_ore_cu.locator: Quoted in Helbig et al. 2020 SI (MMC1) §2.6, p. S7
cu.tailings_share_of_ore_cu.note: Share of copper in mined ore lost to tailings. S11 2011: 3,550 kt of 19,800 kt in ore.

dem.growth_calibration_years.note: Window (years ending 2025) over which the logistic growth rate of per-capita stock is fitted to the historical model run.

dem.population_hold_year.note: Calendar year after which population is held flat (PLAN resolved decision 4). Unit 'a' here denotes a calendar year.

dem.saturation_stock_per_capita.locator: Table 1, pp. 16-17: copper in-use stock per capita, more-developed countries 140-300 kg (determinations mostly 2000-2006)
dem.saturation_stock_per_capita.note: Central value = midpoint of the more-developed-country range; treats today's rich-country stock as the global saturation level (assumption about the future). Same table: global 35-55 kg, less-developed 30-40 kg. Replaces the earlier unsourced 215-300 kg range.

en.depth.energy_per_m.note: Low = Harmsen 2013 (overburden removal, 9 Canadian open pits). High = Pitt & Wadsworth 1980, 4.6 MJ/kg per 100 m at 0.55 % grade, as tabulated in Koppelaar 2016 Table 1.

en.depth.reference_depth.locator: §2.1.5, p. 65 (weighted average depth of present-day mines, from Long 2011)
en.depth.reference_depth.note: Grade-only energy studies already embody mines at this depth; only depth beyond it adds energy.

en.koppelaar.depth_max.note: Range guard. Values beyond these bounds are extrapolations and are logged as warnings.

en.koppelaar.surface.a.locator: Table 5, p. 12, surface mine, milling/flotation, total energy, Eq. (4)

en.koppelaar.surface.b.note: Inverse-grade coefficient with g as a mass fraction. SE 0.0019. R2 = 0.63.

en.koppelaar.surface.c.note: Depth coefficient, SE 0.0002 (p = 0.085, not significant at 5 %).

en.koppelaar.underground.a.locator: Table 5, p. 12, underground, milling/flotation, total energy, Eq. (4)

en.norgate.coarse.a.locator: Values as tabulated in Koppelaar & Koppelaar 2016, Table 1 and text, p. 4
en.norgate.coarse.a.note: Fitted constant term; beneficiation to 75 um plus smelting.

en.norgate.coarse.b.locator: Values as tabulated in Koppelaar & Koppelaar 2016, Table 1 and text, p. 4
en.norgate.coarse.b.note: Grade coefficient with g as a mass fraction (59 MJ/kg per wt% Cu).

en.norgate.fine.a.locator: Values as tabulated in Koppelaar & Koppelaar 2016, Table 1 and text, p. 4
en.norgate.fine.a.note: Fitted constant term; beneficiation to 5 um plus smelting.

en.norgate.fine.b.locator: Values as tabulated in Koppelaar & Koppelaar 2016, Table 1 and text, p. 4
en.norgate.fine.b.note: Grade coefficient with g as a mass fraction (115 MJ/kg per wt% Cu).

en.norgate.grade_max.note: Range guard: warn above this grade.

en.norgate.grade_min.locator: p. 4 (Norgate & Jahanshahi 'established values between a 0.1 and 3.0 % ore grade')
en.norgate.grade_min.note: Range guard: warn below this grade.

geo.calib.produced_share_top500_2010.note: Calibration target for the depth-order multiplier: 85 % of first-km production (526 Mt) from the top 500 m, as a share of total production to ~2010 (580 Mt): 0.85 x 526 / 580.

geo.concentrate_grade.locator: §2.1.3, p. 65 ('a copper concentrate with a grade between 27 % and 30 %')
geo.concentrate_grade.note: Mass fraction of Cu in flotation concentrate; tailings mass = ore - concentrate.

geo.discovered_top500_share_first_km.locator: §2.1.2, p. 64 ('85 % of the reported depth to top ore is within 500 m', from Long 2011)
geo.discovered_top500_share_first_km.note: Used as the share of discovered copper in the first km that lies above 500 m (interpretation: an assumption that depth-to-top-of-ore tracks where the copper is).

geo.discovery_smoothing_years.note: Paced discovery keeps discovered-unmined copper >= lead x the trailing mean of annual extraction over this many years (exploration responds to demand trends, not single years). Introduced to remove a discovery pulse when population is held flat after 2100.

geo.endow.harmsen.analysed_0_1km.note: Discovered deposits with known grade and tonnage; includes copper already produced.

geo.endow.harmsen.layer_4_5km.note: 4-5 km. Layers sum to the table total of 2.49E+04 Mt.

geo.endow.harmsen.produced_0_1km.note: Cumulative production to about 2010 from the first km.

geo.endow.harmsen.produced_share_top_500.note: Share of first-km production assumed to come from the top 500 m.

geo.endow.kesler.above_3_3km.locator: p. 257 ('recoverable resource of ~8.9 x 10^10 t of copper')
geo.endow.kesler.above_3_3km.note: All deposit types above 3.3 km, taken as the likely limit of mining. Enough for ~5,500 years of 2008 mine production.

geo.endow.kesler.depth_limit.locator: p. 257 ('assuming ~3.3 km as the likely limit of mining')
geo.endow.kesler.depth_limit.note: Kesler bracket uses Harmsen's depth profile, truncated here and scaled to 89 Bt (assumption: Kesler & Wilkinson give no depth distribution).

geo.grade.gerst.mu_w.note: Location parameter of ln(grade, wt%). Gerst reports median 0.52 %, mean 0.56 %. Porphyry deposits only; sediment-hosted (mu_w 0.4269) and VMS (-0.3949) differ and may make the true global distribution bimodal.

geo.grade.kesler_ext.mu_w.locator: p. 623, text following eqs 16-17 (extrapolation to Kesler & Wilkinson endowment)
geo.grade.kesler_ext.mu_w.note: Grade distribution extrapolated to the larger Kesler & Wilkinson 2008 resource.

geo.grade.kesler_ext.sigma2_w.locator: p. 623, text following eqs 16-17 (extrapolation to Kesler & Wilkinson endowment)

geo.max_discovery_rate.note: Diminishing discovery (Steve, 2026-10-15): annual discovery capped at this share of the copper still undiscovered (exploration 'creaming'). At 0.01 the cap binds only once roughly 70 % of the Harmsen endowment has been discovered. Unsourced assumption.

geo.strip_ratio.locator: Results: copper's attributable ore mined + waste rock removed = 9.4 Bt (2018)
geo.strip_ratio.note: Waste rock per tonne ore = (9.4 Bt - model 2018 ore 3.8 Bt) / 3.8 Bt = 1.47. Revenue-allocated (Cu-Au and Cu-Mo mines share burdens), so a physical lower bound. High = the conventional strip ratio of 2 used in total-material-requirement studies and as Nassar's surface-mine default.

geo.tailings_dry_density.locator: Table 1, 'Natural dry density' (sand cone): dam zone 1.39-1.48, pond zone 1.30-1.44 t/m3
geo.tailings_dry_density.note: In-situ dry density of a decades-old conventional (slurry) copper TSF in Chile; value is the midpoint of the combined in-situ range. Laboratory limits from the same table: standard-Proctor maximum 1.94 (dam) / 1.80 (pond), minimum 1.30; specific gravity 2.72-2.79. Proctor maxima are an upper bound for compacted or filtered (dry-stack) storage, not conventional ponds. Single-site evidence.

geo.usgs.identified.note: Identified resources at the 2013 assessment. MCS 2026 (citing the 2015 assessment, Hammarstrom et al. 2019) states the 2.1 Bt INCLUDES ~600 Mt of past production, i.e. ~1.5 Bt unextracted; see geo.usgs.identified_unextracted.

geo.usgs.identified_unextracted.note: Identified resources excluding ~600 Mt past production (2015 assessment, Hammarstrom et al. 2019).

geo.usgs.undiscovered_mean.note: Mean undiscovered: porphyry within 1 km, sediment-hosted stratabound within 2.5 km of surface.

st.allocation_pinch.note: How copper is spread over products before tolerances bind. 0 = mixed: as evenly as tolerances allow, close to Daehn's 2008 Sankey where EAF steel goes to products pro rata (EAF share of construction 38 %, vehicles 16 %; SI Table S24). 1 = pinch: most tolerant products first (Daehn's perfect-allocation analysis), which concentrates copper in long-lived construction steel. Primary iron and unusable scrap are the same either way; only where copper sits, and so what returns decades later, differs.

st.cu_to_process_losses.note: Share of the copper concentration carried by the process-loss allowance (slag, dust, unrecovered yield losses). 0 = copper stays with the steel, since it is more noble than iron and does not oxidise into slag; tolerance then applies to product mass, as in Daehn Fig. 2 (1.8 Mt tolerable in 2008). 1 = losses carry copper at melt concentration, as in Daehn Fig. 3.

st.dri_share_of_primary.locator: Fig. 1 (2008): direct reduction DRI 66 Mt of pig iron 928 + DRI 66 Mt
st.dri_share_of_primary.note: Share of primary iron made by direct reduction; held constant (assumption). Bounds are an assumption (DRI output has roughly doubled since 2008).

st.energy.bf_bof.locator: Table 2.1.2, p. 7: BF-BOF integrated steel, total primary energy (low = thin-slab casting alternative)

st.energy.dri_eaf.locator: Table 2.1.2, p. 7: DRI-EAF, total primary energy (low = thin-slab casting alternative; best-practice DRI is coal-based SL/RN, Section 2.1.3)

st.energy.scrap_eaf.locator: Table 2.1.2, p. 7: scrap-based EAF, total primary energy (low = thin-slab casting alternative)

st.eol_recovery_rate.locator: p. 6601: '80% (average end-of-life recovery rate)', citing worldsteel 2010 fact sheet
st.eol_recovery_rate.note: Share of end-of-life steel recovered as scrap; the rest stays in obsolete stocks or landfill. Low bound: Pauliuk et al. 2013b p. 29 (iii) assume ca. 30 % of steel leaving use is lost to landfill or obsolete stocks. High bound 0.90: UNEP/Daehn p. 6599 cites recovery 'as high as 90%'.

st.lifetime.construction.locator: Table 4 basic set; bounds = Table 4 'construction lifetime 33% shorter/longer' (50, 100 a). Daehn et al. 2017 p. 6601 uses the same 75 a

st.lifetime.industrial_equipment.locator: Table 4 basic set (also Pauliuk et al. 2013a Table 1, all regions except developed Asia); bounds = Table 4 'all lifetimes 33% shorter/longer'

st.lifetime.metal_goods.locator: Table 4 basic set (also Pauliuk et al. 2013a Table 1, all regions except developed Asia); bounds = Table 4 'all lifetimes 33% shorter/longer'

st.lifetime.transport.locator: Table 4 basic set (also Pauliuk et al. 2013a Table 1, all regions except developed Asia); bounds = Table 4 'all lifetimes 33% shorter/longer'

st.lifetime_sigma_fraction.locator: Section 2.3.3, p. 26: 'the lifetime followed a normal distribution and the standard deviation was set to 30% of the mean'

st.process_loss_allowance.locator: p. 6602, Section 2.2: 'an overall average of 12% was added to each product category to cover these losses'
st.process_loss_allowance.note: Iron sources charged per tonne of product = 1 + this. Copper leaving with these losses is assumed to be at the melt concentration.

st.product_yield.locator: Fig. 1: steel end-use products 1,088 Mt less cast iron 68 and cast steel 10 = 1,010 Mt; world crude steel 2008 1,330 Mt (USGS DS140)
st.product_yield.note: Final steel products per tonne of crude steel; converts the historical crude-steel series into product inflow.

st.saturation_stock_per_capita.metal_goo.locator: Table 6, p. 29: appliances and other 0.6 +/- 0.2 t/person
st.saturation_stock_per_capita.metal_goo.note: Total 13.4 t/person ('13 +/- 2', Table 6). Sectors are sampled independently in Monte Carlo, which widens the total range slightly beyond +/- 2 t.

st.saturation_stock_per_capita.transport.locator: Table 6, p. 29: transportation 1.5 +/- 0.7 t/person (mature stocks); Pauliuk et al. 2013a Table 1 uses 1.5

st.share.transport.note: Pauliuk et al. 2013a 2008 final demand by sector (1,037 Mt) as tabulated by Daehn. Cullen et al. 2012 gives 139/176/596/177 of 1,088 Mt; Pauliuk's split is used because lifetimes and saturation levels are his. Held constant over 1900-2025 (assumption); Daehn combines Pauliuk's sector demand with Cullen's product matrix in the same way (SI 2.2.1.1).

st.target.construction_stock_share.locator: p. 3451: 'Construction accounts for 75% of the stocks, followed by transportation (ca. 10%) and machinery (ca. 8%)'

st.target.final_demand_2008.note: Validation target (Mt/yr). Pauliuk's final demand counts all steel-containing products; the model's product inflow excludes castings.
